results.root_cause_actual: PR #881 (api-gateway v9.2.0) simultaneously raised the payments-svc read timeout from 3s to 30s and disabled the circuit breaker, removing both fast-fail protections. When the partner acquirer p99 latency rose to 12.4s at 18:47Z (a pre-existing degradation), each payment request now held a gateway worker thread for up to ~30s instead of failing fast at 3s. The critical value mismatch is that the ALB proxy_read_timeout remained at 10s while the gateway upstream read timeout was now 30s: the ALB killed the client-facing connection at 10s, but the gateway thread continued blocking on the upstream connection for the full ~30s (observed 29.9s). With a fixed pool of only 64 worker threads and each thread held ~30s, incoming payment requests accumulated faster than threads could be freed, driving threads_busy from 9 to 64/64 and the accept queue to 611. With all threads blocked in PaymentsClient.execute(), routes with no dependency on payments-svc (/v1/orders, /v1/catalog) also began returning 504 due to thread starvation, dropping overall gateway availability to 88.1% and generating 4180 ALB 504s in one minute.
results.root_cause_expected: PR #881 raised the gateway's payments-svc read timeout from 3s to 30s (and disabled the circuit breaker) while the edge load balancer's proxy_read_timeout stayed at 10s. When partner latency rose, the edge cut clients off at 10s with 504s while gateway worker threads stayed pinned on the upstream call for the full 30s, saturating the 64-thread pool and taking down routes that never touch payments-svc.

judge.reason: Both identify the same underlying cause: PR #881's mismatch between the gateway's 30s read timeout and the ALB's 10s proxy_read_timeout, combined with disabling the circuit breaker, which caused worker thread starvation when partner latency increased.

ruled_out.candidate: Partner acquirer latency degradation (ACQ-3391) as the root cause
ruled_out.why_not: The partner degradation is a pre-existing condition; under v9.1.7 with a 3s timeout and enabled circuit breaker, calls failed fast and caused no incident. The degradation only became an incident-causing factor because v9.2.0 removed both fast-fail mechanisms.

ruled_out.candidate: payments-svc itself being unhealthy or failing
ruled_out.why_not: payments-svc reported healthy throughout: 5xx rate 0.03%, CPU 34%, no deploy since 2026-08-15. Thread saturation was observed in PaymentsClient (gateway-side client), and /v1/orders and /v1/catalog failed despite never calling payments-svc.

ruled_out.candidate: Traffic volume spike overwhelming the thread pool
ruled_out.why_not: Notable absence explicitly states 'No indication of traffic volume spike; thread exhaustion appears driven by held connections, not request rate surge.' Gateway CPU also dropped to 8% post-deploy despite thread saturation, indicating threads are idle-waiting, not CPU-bound.

ruled_out.candidate: ALB proxy_read_timeout (10s) being the root cause change
ruled_out.why_not: The ALB timeout has been 10s since 2024 and was explicitly not changed by PR #881. It is a contributing factor to the mismatch but not itself a new change that caused the incident.

red_herrings.candidate: Traffic volume spike overwhelming the thread pool
red_herrings.why_not: gateway_cpu_pct dropped from 27% to 8% after deploy (metrics.json), indicating threads are idle-waiting on I/O, not CPU-bound from high request volume. The deploy record and artifacts contain no mention of a traffic spike.

red_herrings.candidate: Partner acquirer latency degradation (ACQ-3391) alone as root cause
red_herrings.why_not: Partner acquirer latency p99 rose from 1.9s to 12.4s at 18:47Z (known partner degradation, ticket ACQ-3391). Under v9.1.7 these calls failed fast at 3s — confirming the degradation was pre-existing and only became incident-causing because PR #881 removed both fast-fail mechanisms.

red_herrings.candidate: ALB proxy_read_timeout (10s) being the root cause change
red_herrings.why_not: alb-prod proxy_read_timeout = 10s — This value has been 10s since 2024 and was not touched by PR #881. It is an unchanged value that forms the mismatched pair with the newly raised 30s upstream timeout, but it is not itself the change that caused the incident.

cross_file_value_checks.governs: client-facing connection lifetime vs. gateway upstream hold time on payment calls
cross_file_value_checks.note: ALB drops the client connection at 10s, but the gateway thread continues holding the upstream payments-svc connection for up to 30s. The thread is consumed for ~30s despite the client already being gone, enabling thread accumulation.

cross_file_value_checks.governs: thread pool capacity vs. per-request hold duration under degraded acquirer conditions
cross_file_value_checks.note: With each payment thread held ~30s and a fixed pool of 64 threads, even modest payment request rates saturate the pool. At p99=29.9s, the pool drains in seconds of sustained traffic.

cross_file_value_checks.governs: whether payment calls fail fast or block threads on slow acquirer responses
cross_file_value_checks.note: 30s timeout is far above the 12.4s acquirer p99, so calls do not time out quickly. Under v9.1.7 the 3s timeout was below the degraded p99 (12.4s), causing fast failure rather than thread accumulation.

cross_file_value_checks.governs: fast-fail behaviour of gateway under acquirer degradation before PR #881
cross_file_value_checks.note: 3s < 12.4s, so pre-deploy the timeout fired before the acquirer responded, failing fast and preventing thread accumulation. This confirms the old config protected against the acquirer degradation scenario.

cross_file_value_checks.governs: request backlog once all worker threads are saturated
cross_file_value_checks.note: All 64 threads blocked; 611 requests queued. The queue continues to grow because no threads are available to drain it, affecting all routes including those with no dependency on payments-svc.

cross_file_value_checks.governs: second fast-fail protection removed alongside timeout increase
cross_file_value_checks.note: Disabling the circuit breaker removed the only remaining fast-fail mechanism after the timeout was raised to 30s, leaving no protection against sustained acquirer latency.
